subject: Hidden clues could help predict a woman's breast cancer risk years in advance
posts:
AI mammogram research unlocks early breast cancer risk detection years ahead of clinical symptoms.
Evidence: peer-reviewed study, 313k scans, NYU Langone
#Health #AI #MedicalScience

An artificial intelligence tool developed at NYU Langone analyzes years of 3D mammograms to predict breast cancer risk up to five years prior.
Stated Judgement: (+0.8, +0.6) — Lesser Good

Researchers published study findings in the American Journal of Roentgenology using 313k scans, though experts note it requires multi-center testing and lacks FDA approval.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.7, +0.8) — Lesser Good

Verdict: PASS — The Path of Redemption.
Rigorous medical research provides early screening tools while openly acknowledging necessary clinical validation stages.

Integrity: Trustworthy (Hypocrisy: 1.2, Uncertainty z: 1)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- NYU Langone Research: PASS (+0.8, +0.8) — Validated peer-reviewed study.
- Media Reporting: PASS (+0.6, +0.6) — Accurate nuance on limitations.
Researchers at NYU Langone Health developed an AI model that reviews multi-year 3D mammograms to track breast tissue changes and estimate five-year cancer risks.

The Poison:
Media coverage occasionally frames early AI research as an immediate clinical diagnostic tool before multi-center validation is complete.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Confusing a research-stage predictive model (WHAT) with an FDA-approved diagnostic replacement (WHO/HOW).

Social Physics Analysis:
Researchers and medical experts operate within a transparent empirical loop, sharing data openly while clearly defining clinical boundaries and limitations.

The Trajectory: The Path of Redemption.
When medical research aligns transparent methodology with empirical validation, it charts a direct course toward human empowerment and better health outcomes.

The Unavoidable Truth: AI analysis of historical mammograms can identify subtle tissue changes preceding clinical tumors.

The Unavoidable Lie: Algorithmic risk scores currently replace the need for physical diagnostic biopsies or regular exams.

AI technology is transforming breast cancer screening by assisting doctors in identifying women at higher risk years before cancer develops. Mount Sinai's Breast Surgery Director and author of 'The Breast Advice' Dr. Elisa Port highlights how AI uncovers hidden tumors and slashes false positive results, especially for women with dense breasts. This advancement aims to increase screening adherence among the 30-40% who currently don't get regular mammograms.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.

The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.

NEW ALZHEIMER'S BLOOD TEST PREDICTS WHO IS LIKELY TO DEVELOP DEMENTIA IN 5 TO 10 YEARS

The model was developed using more than 313,000 mammograms from more than 161,000 women, according to the study.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance. (iStock)

Connie Lehman, a Massachusetts-based breast imaging specialist and professor of radiology at Harvard Medical School who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that AI could help identify women whose increased risk might otherwise go unnoticed.

"For decades, as a doctor and breast imaging specialist, I have cared for women who were shocked by a breast cancer diagnosis," Lehman said. "Again and again, I heard: 'How can this be? No one in my family has had breast cancer.'"

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues within a woman's breast tissue, according to Lehman.

The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time. (iStock)

"A mammogram can tell us more than whether cancer is visible today — it can also provide information about a woman's risk of developing cancer in the years ahead," she said.

That information could eventually help doctors tailor breast cancer screening to a woman's individual risk, Lehman said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

Women identified as being at increased risk could discuss additional screening, such as MRI, with their health care providers, while women at average risk may continue with routine mammograms, according to Lehman.

The technology could also analyze mammograms a woman has already had, meaning the added risk information would not require another imaging exam or additional radiation, she noted.

Traditional risk assessments can consider factors such as family history and genetic mutations, while AI can look for additional clues in a woman's breast tissue, experts say. (iStock)

Lehman cautioned that an AI risk score is not a cancer diagnosis and cannot predict with certainty whether a woman will develop the disease.

"A higher score can prompt a conversation with your health care provider about additional screening and risk-reduction options," she said. "A lower score does not eliminate risk or replace regular mammography."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The NYU model remains a research tool and is not FDA-authorized for clinical use, according to Lehman.

The researchers also noted that more testing is needed. The study used mammograms from NYU Langone hospitals and imaging equipment from one manufacturer.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The team plans to test the model using data from other medical centers and different 3D mammography systems, according to NYU Langone.

Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.
